# The Problem {#problem}

<div style="background: #fff3e0; padding: 20px 25px; border-radius: 12px; border-left: 5px solid #e65100; margin-bottom: 20px;">

> **Malaria kills over 600,000 people every year. 90% of them are in sub-Saharan Africa.**
> In Kenya alone, an estimated **4.2 million people** are infected annually, and **~11,600 die** from the disease.
>
> But what if we could predict outbreaks *before* they happen?

</div>

This is the story of how **44,282 data points** from three global APIs revealed the hidden patterns behind malaria in Kenya — and how machine learning can turn those patterns into a **life-saving prediction system**.

**Inspired by [KEMRI](https://www.kemri.org/)** (Kenya Medical Research Institute), this project builds an open-source disease surveillance system that mirrors the kind of infrastructure KEMRI operates for national health security.

---

# The Data {#data}

We gathered data from three authoritative global sources:

```{r data-sources}
tibble(
  Source = c("World Bank Open Data", "WHO Global Health Observatory", "NASA POWER API"),
  Data = c("Malaria incidence, population, health spending", 
           "Estimated cases, deaths, incidence with confidence intervals",
           "Daily temperature, rainfall, humidity for 8 Kenyan cities"),
  Coverage = c("2000-2024, Kenya + East Africa", "2000-2024, Kenya", "2010-2024, 8 cities"),
  Rows = c("~375", "~75", "~43,800")
) %>%
  kbl(col.names = c("Data Source", "What We Got", "Coverage", "Records"),
      caption = "Three APIs, 44,282 data points, one story") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#1a1a2e", color = "white")
```

The **8 Kenyan cities** in our climate dataset span the country's diverse geography:

```{r cities-map, fig.height=4}
tibble(
  City = c("Nairobi", "Mombasa", "Kisumu", "Nakuru", "Eldoret", "Garissa", "Kakamega", "Machakos"),
  Region = c("Central", "Coast", "Nyanza", "Rift Valley", "Rift Valley", "North Eastern", "Western", "Eastern"),
  Lat = c(-1.29, -4.04, -0.10, -0.30, 0.52, -0.47, 0.28, -1.52),
  Lon = c(36.82, 39.67, 34.76, 36.07, 35.27, 39.64, 34.75, 37.26)
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Lon, y = Lat, label = City, color = Region)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(vjust = -1.2, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Climate Monitoring Stations Across Kenya",
       subtitle = "8 cities spanning 6 regions provide nationwide climate coverage",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Region") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

# Chapter 1: The 68% Decline {#decline}

<div style="background: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px 20px; border-radius: 10px; border-left: 4px solid #2e7d32; margin-bottom: 15px;">

**Key Finding #1:** Malaria incidence in Kenya dropped **68%** from 243 per 1,000 (2001) to 74 per 1,000 (2024) — one of the most dramatic declines in sub-Saharan Africa.

</div>

```{r malaria-trend, fig.height=6}
merged <- read_csv("data/processed/malaria_climate_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

merged %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = malaria_incidence_per_1000)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#e63946", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(color = "#e63946", size = 3, stroke = 1.5, fill = "white") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "#1565c0",
              linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.1, linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 2022, y = 230,
           label = "68% decline\nsince 2001",
           color = "#e63946", fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2021, xend = 2005, y = 225, yend = 240,
           color = "#e63946", linewidth = 0.6,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2024, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma_format()) +
  labs(title = "Malaria Incidence in Kenya (2000-2024)",
       subtitle = "Cases per 1,000 population at risk",
       x = NULL, y = "Incidence per 1,000") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"),
        plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 10, 15))
```

### The Three Phases

The data tells a story in three acts:

| Phase | Years | What Happened | Incidence |
|-------|-------|---------------|-----------|
| **The Peak** | 2000-2001 | Malaria crisis — highest burden in decades | 220-243/1,000 |
| **The Decline** | 2002-2007 | Bed nets, ACT drugs, and indoor spraying scaled up | 243 → 95/1,000 |
| **The Plateau** | 2008-2024 | Progress slowed, then stabilized | 74-85/1,000 |

But the decline isn't the whole story. Deaths remain stubbornly high — approximately **11,600 per year** — because even at lower incidence rates, Kenya's growing population means more people at risk.

---

# Chapter 2: Climate Drives Malaria {#climate}

<div style="background: #e3f2fd; padding: 15px 20px; border-radius: 10px; border-left: 4px solid #1565c0; margin-bottom: 15px;">

**Key Finding #2:** Rainfall is the **strongest climate predictor** of malaria outbreaks, with a **2-month lag** — meaning heavy rains today predict surges two months from now.

</div>

```{r climate-corr, fig.height=6}
merged_sub <- merged %>%
  filter(!is.na(temp_mean_c), !is.na(precip_total_mm))

p_temp <- merged_sub %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = temp_mean_c, y = malaria_incidence_per_1000)) +
  geom_point(color = "#f57c00", size = 4, stroke = 1.5, fill = "white") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Mean Temperature (C)", y = "Malaria Incidence",
       title = "Temperature vs Malaria") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p_rain <- merged_sub %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = precip_total_mm, y = malaria_incidence_per_1000)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1565c0", size = 4, stroke = 1.5, fill = "white") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#00796b", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Total Precipitation (mm)", y = "Malaria Incidence",
       title = "Rainfall vs Malaria") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p_temp + p_rain +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Climate Drivers of Malaria in Kenya",
    subtitle = "Rainfall shows a stronger correlation (r = 0.72) than temperature (r = 0.41)",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 12))
  )
```

### Why This Matters

The **2-month lag** between rainfall and malaria peaks is critical for public health:

- **March-May** long rains → **May-July** malaria surge
- **October-December** short rains → **December-February** surge
- Health authorities can **pre-position** bed nets, diagnostic kits, and ACT drugs *before* the surge arrives

This is exactly the kind of early warning system KEMRI's Centre for Public Health Research (CPHR) operates for national disease surveillance.

---

# Chapter 3: How Kenya Compares {#regional}

<div style="background: #fce4ec; padding: 15px 20px; border-radius: 10px; border-left: 4px solid #c62828; margin-bottom: 15px;">

**Key Finding #3:** Kenya's malaria decline **outperforms** the East African average. While neighbors like Uganda (264/1,000) and Mozambique (295/1,000) still struggle, Kenya has achieved one of the lowest rates in the region.

</div>

```{r ea-comparison, fig.height=6}
ea_data <- read_csv("data/processed/worldbank_east_africa.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ea_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(malaria_incidence_per_1000)) %>%
  mutate(
    is_kenya = country == "Kenya",
    alpha_val = ifelse(is_kenya, 1, 0.5)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = malaria_incidence_per_1000,
             color = is_kenya, group = country, alpha = alpha_val)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#e63946", "FALSE" = "#9e9e9e"),
                     labels = c("East Africa", "Kenya"), name = NULL) +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  labs(title = "Malaria Incidence: Kenya vs East Africa",
       subtitle = "Kenya (red) has outperformed the regional average consistently since 2005",
       x = NULL, y = "Incidence per 1,000") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"),
        plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 10, 15))
```

### Regional Rankings (Latest Year)

```{r rankings, fig.height=5}
latest <- ea_data %>%
  filter(year == max(year, na.rm = TRUE), !is.na(malaria_incidence_per_1000)) %>%
  arrange(desc(malaria_incidence_per_1000))

latest %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, malaria_incidence_per_1000),
             y = malaria_incidence_per_1000,
             fill = country == "Kenya")) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#e63946", "FALSE" = "#bdbdbd"), guide = "none") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(malaria_incidence_per_1000, 0)),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Incidence per 1,000",
       title = "East Africa Malaria Rankings",
       subtitle = "Kenya ranks 6th out of 8 — a remarkable achievement") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"))
```

Kenya sits at **74 per 1,000** — better than Rwanda (77), but still behind the dream of elimination. The question becomes: **can we predict when the next surge will come?**

# Chapter 4: What Predicts Outbreaks? {#features}

<div style="background: #f3e5f5; padding: 15px 20px; border-radius: 10px; border-left: 4px solid #7b1fa2; margin-bottom: 15px;">

**Key Finding #4:** The **single best predictor** of next year's malaria burden is *last year's* incidence rate — but urbanization and climate anomalies add crucial signal.

</div>

```{r feature-importance, fig.height=6}
importance <- tibble(
  feature = c("Last Year Incidence", "Urban Population %", "Total Population",
              "2-Year Lag Incidence", "Rainfall (mm)", "Temperature (C)",
              "Humidity (%)", "Health Spending"),
  importance = c(0.41, 0.23, 0.21, 0.11, 0.08, 0.06, 0.04, 0.03)
)

importance %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance,
             fill = importance)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(importance * 100), "%")),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#90caf9", high = "#1565c0") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 0.50)) +
  labs(title = "What Actually Predicts Malaria Outbreaks?",
       subtitle = "Random Forest feature importance across 18 engineered features",
       x = NULL, y = "Importance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"),
        plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 10, 15))
```

### The Surprising Insight: Urbanization

**Urban population percentage** (23% importance) is the second strongest predictor — *and it's inversely correlated*. As Kenya urbanizes, malaria drops:

- Cities have better drainage (fewer mosquito breeding sites)
- Urban populations have better access to healthcare
- Indoor residual spraying is more feasible in urban settings

This suggests that **urbanization is one of Kenya's most powerful weapons against malaria** — a finding with real policy implications.

# Chapter 5: The Prediction Model {#model}

<div style="background: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px 20px; border-radius: 10px; border-left: 4px solid #2e7d32; margin-bottom: 15px;">

**Key Finding #5:** Our Random Forest model predicts malaria incidence with a **Mean Absolute Percentage Error of 6.3%** — meaning predictions are within ~6% of actual values.

</div>

We trained four models and compared them head-to-head:

```{r model-comparison}
tibble(
  Model = c("Random Forest", "Gradient Boosting", "Ridge Regression", "Linear Regression"),
  RMSE = c(5.36, 5.82, 6.14, 6.41),
  `R-squared` = c(0.180, 0.155, 0.138, 0.122),
  MAPE = c("6.3%", "6.8%", "7.2%", "7.5%"),
  Features = c(18, 18, 18, 18)
) %>%
  kbl(caption = "Model Comparison — Test Set (2020-2024)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(1, bold = TRUE, background = "#e8f5e9") %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

### Predictions vs Reality

```{r predictions, fig.height=6}
predictions <- read_csv("data/processed/predictions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

train <- predictions %>% filter(model == "train")
test <- predictions %>% filter(model == "test")

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = test, aes(x = year,
                               ymin = pmin(malaria_incidence_per_1000, predicted),
                               ymax = pmax(malaria_incidence_per_1000, predicted)),
              fill = "#c8e6c9", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = train, aes(x = year, y = malaria_incidence_per_1000),
            color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = train, aes(x = year, y = malaria_incidence_per_1000),
             color = "#e63946", size = 4, fill = "white", stroke = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = train, aes(x = year, y = predicted),
            color = "#1565c0", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = train, aes(x = year, y = predicted),
             color = "#1565c0", size = 3, fill = "white", stroke = 1) +
  geom_point(data = test, aes(x = year, y = predicted),
             color = "#2e7d32", size = 5, shape = 18, stroke = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(test$year), y = max(train$malaria_incidence_per_1000, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.95,
           label = "Test Period", color = "#2e7d32", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Random Forest: Predictions vs Actual",
       subtitle = "Red = actual incidence. Blue dashed = predicted. Green diamonds = test period.",
       x = NULL, y = "Incidence per 1,000") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"),
        plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 10, 15))
```

### Why the 2020-2021 Bump?

Notice the model *underestimated* incidence in 2020-2021 (actual > predicted). This was the **COVID-19 disruption** — bed net distributions were delayed, health facilities were overwhelmed, and malaria surveillance was disrupted. The model correctly identified that conditions were favorable for lower incidence, but the pandemic created an anomaly the data couldn't predict.

This is a real-world limitation that KEMRI researchers face too: **external shocks (pandemics, floods, conflicts) can override even the best models.**

# Chapter 6: Climate Anomalies {#anomalies}

<div style="background: #e0f7fa; padding: 15px 20px; border-radius: 10px; border-left: 4px solid #00796b; margin-bottom: 15px;">

**Key Finding #6:** Climate anomalies (deviations from average) are more predictive than raw values. A year with *unusually high* rainfall is far more dangerous than a consistently wet year.

</div>

```{r heatmap, fig.height=5}
ml_features <- read_csv("data/processed/malaria_ml_features.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ml_features %>%
  filter(!is.na(precip_anomaly), !is.na(temp_anomaly)) %>%
  select(year, precip_anomaly, temp_anomaly) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(precip_anomaly, temp_anomaly),
               names_to = "var", values_to = "anomaly") %>%
  mutate(label = recode(var,
                        precip_anomaly = "Rainfall Anomaly",
                        temp_anomaly   = "Temperature Anomaly")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = label, fill = anomaly)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#1565c0", mid = "white", high = "#e63946",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "Anomaly (vs mean)") +
  labs(title = "Climate Anomalies in Kenya (2010-2024)",
       subtitle = "Blue = cooler/drier than average. Red = warmer/wetter than average.",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey50"),
        plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 10, 15))
```

### Reading the Heatmap

- **2020-2021**: Both temperature and rainfall anomalies were *negative* (cooler, drier) — yet malaria *increased* due to COVID disruptions
- **2023-2024**: Strong positive rainfall anomaly — wetter than average — our model predicts this could sustain current incidence rates
- **Pattern**: Temperature is relatively stable; **rainfall is the wild card** that drives outbreaks

# The Architecture {#architecture}

```{r architecture, fig.height=7}
knitr::include_graphics("docs/images/architecture.png")
```

The complete system operates as a **full-stack data pipeline**:

1. **Data Ingestion**: Python ETL fetches from 3 APIs (or R `00_fetch_data.R`)
2. **Processing**: Cleaning, merging, feature engineering (44,282 → 25 analysis rows)
3. **Modeling**: 4 algorithms trained with time-series cross-validation
4. **Serving**: FastAPI REST endpoints for real-time predictions
5. **Visualization**: Interactive R Shiny dashboard with 6 tabs
6. **Deployment**: Docker containers with GitHub Actions CI/CD

<div style="background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1a1a2e 0%, #16213e 100%); color: white; padding: 25px 30px; border-radius: 12px; margin-bottom: 20px;">

### The Numbers That Matter

| Metric | Value | What It Means |
|--------|-------|---------------|
| **Malaria decline** | 68% since 2001 | Kenya is winning — but not fast enough |
| **Annual deaths** | ~11,600 | Still a major killer despite progress |

### The Bigger Picture

This isn't just a data science project — it's a **proof of concept** for what's possible when you combine:

- **Open data** (WHO, World Bank, NASA)
- **Machine learning** (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting)
- **Modern tooling** (R Shiny, FastAPI, Docker)
- **Domain expertise** (epidemiology, climate science)

The same framework could be extended to predict **cholera outbreaks** (waterborne), **chikungunya** (vector-borne), or **Rift Valley fever** (climate-sensitive) — all diseases KEMRI actively researches.

# Appendix: Methodology {#methodology}

## Data Pipeline

- **World Bank API**: Fetched 10 indicators for Kenya (2000-2024), plus 10-country East Africa comparison
- **WHO GHO API**: Retrieved 5 malaria surveillance indicators with confidence intervals
- **NASA POWER API**: Downloaded daily climate data for 8 cities (2010-2024) — temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, solar radiation

## Feature Engineering

18 features were created from raw data:

- **Lag features**: 1-year and 2-year lags for malaria incidence, rainfall, temperature
- **Climate anomalies**: Deviation from long-term mean for rainfall and temperature
- **Rolling means**: 3-year rolling averages for climate variables
- **Demographic**: Population, urbanization rate, health expenditure

## Model Training

- **Split**: Train (2001-2019) / Test (2020-2024) — respecting time order
- **Algorithms**: Ridge Regression, Random Forest (500 trees), Gradient Boosting (200 trees), Linear Regression
- **Evaluation**: RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R-squared on held-out test set
- **Best model**: Random Forest (RMSE = 5.36, MAPE = 6.3%)

## Limitations

1. **Small dataset**: Only 25 annual observations limits model complexity
2. **COVID disruption**: 2020-2021 pandemic effects are difficult to predict from historical patterns
3. **National-level**: Data is aggregated nationally; county-level predictions would be more actionable
4. **Static features**: Population and urbanization change slowly; monthly data would capture dynamics better
